analysis.investment_thesis: MedPlus trades at a price roughly 4× its estimated Graham Number (~₹208), with a P/E of 51× and P/B of 5.7× — both catastrophically above my maximum thresholds of 15× and 1.5× respectively. The thin 4.75% operating margin, volatile net profit history, and zero dividends offer no margin of safety whatsoever.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 15.1% over nine years shows genuine business growth
OCF positive in all last 5 years with a strong FY2025 FCF of ₹482 Cr — a meaningful recent improvement
Long operating track record since 2006 provides some earnings history, unlike pure IPO speculations
key_risks: Valuation is extreme: P/E 51× vs my ceiling of 15×; Graham Number ≈ ₹208 implies 76% downside to fair value
Net profit has been wildly erratic — ₹2 Cr in FY2020, ₹50 Cr in FY2023 vs ₹95 Cr prior year — no stable earnings power
Debt rising steadily to ₹1,193 Cr borrowings with only ₹86 Cr cash; D/E of 0.65 breaches my 0.50 limit and finance costs compound at 22% CAGR
red_flags: P/E of 50.9× is 3.4× my maximum acceptable multiple
P/B of 5.7× is nearly 4× my ceiling of 1.5× — paying an enormous premium over tangible assets
Graham Number estimated at ~₹208 (sqrt[22.5 × ₹12.5 EPS × ₹154 BVPS]) vs market price of ₹878 — a 320% premium
No dividends — zero cash returned to shareholders despite a decade of operations
ROE of only 8.8% on an inflated book value signals poor capital allocation
analysis.detailed_analysis:
MedPlus is a pharmacy retail chain earning thin 4.75% operating margins on ₹6,136 Cr of revenue. Through my quantitative lens, the numbers are disqualifying across every dimension. The Graham Number, the most fundamental test I apply, works out to approximately ₹208 per share (√[22.5 × ~₹12.5 EPS × ~₹154 BVPS]) against a market price of ₹878 — the stock must fall over 75% just to reach my definition of fair value. A P/E of 51× and P/B of 5.7× are not merely elevated; they reflect pure speculation on future growth that has not yet materialised in the bottom line.

The earnings history further disqualifies this as a Graham investment. Net profit collapsed to ₹2 Cr in FY2020 and again fell from ₹95 Cr to ₹50 Cr in FY2023 — this is not the steady, predictable earning power I require over a minimum five-year span. Mr. Market has attached a premium as if this were a dominant, high-margin franchise, yet the business earns only 8.8% ROE and 10.3% ROCE while borrowings compound at 22% annually. The FY2025 FCF surge to ₹482 Cr is encouraging but represents a single data point, not the proven earning power I demand before deploying capital. The intelligent investor must insist on a margin of safety — here, none exists.
